title: In-custody death probe starts today
article: The coroner's inquest into the death of Cheryl Ann Bouey will start today.

"Ms. Bouey died in police custody in cells at the Prince George RCMP detachment on June 26, 2008," said a spokesperson for the B.C. Coroner's Service. "Presiding coroner Rodrick MacKenzie and a jury will publicly hear evidence from subpoenaed witnesses in order to determine the facts surrounding the death. The jury will have the opportunity to make recommendations aimed at preventing deaths under similar circumstances in the future."
It is expected that pathology and toxicology evidence will be heard, allowing the public to hear for the first time what the cause of Bouey's death was.
At the time of the incident, Prince George RCMP said the death was, in their view, a suicide.
"The first officer on the scene cut a small string that was around her neck and around the bars while she was in the sitting position," said RCMP Staff Sgt. Tom Bethune.
"It is similar to the string you would find sewn into the belt-line of a pair of track pants, like a bathing-suit tie.
"It is our belief that she tied that string herself, a self-inflicted injury that caused her death."
Coroner's inquests are almost automatic when someone dies in police custody.

"The complete incident was recorded on video from the time she arrived at the detachment until the time she left in the ambulance. She was never out of video surveillance. Everything is on video," Bethune said.

"At times the female was argumentative with police and her spouse (taken into custody at the same time for public drunkenness), but was not really physically combative. She was placed in the female drunk tank by herself. It is a room that is basically barren. It has a toilet and it has bars for a gate, that's it."
According to RCMP, all cells must be checked on an irregular pattern that allows no more than 15 minutes to elapse between personal observations.
Bethune said these routine checks were being done by the attending guard.

"The guard noted during the normal checks that she was sitting up against the bars, and it is not uncommon for drunks to sit there like that. On further check, it appeared that she seemed unresponsive.
"He immediately sounded the alarm, summoned myself and other police officers and we were there in seconds. The female was indeed unresponsive, and we called the ambulance."
The incident is also under investigation internally by the RCMP and also by the independent Commission for Public Complaints Against the RCMP.
Testimony begins after the swearing in of the jury at 9:30 a.m. today at the Prince George court house. The inquest is scheduled to run until Nov.6.
